claims.text: Atomic structure, dislocation dynamics, and grain-boundary properties jointly govern the mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Dislocation dynamics contribute to the high-temperature strength of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary properties contribute to the enhanced strength of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Atomic structure, dislocation dynamics, and grain-boundary properties enhance creep resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Atomic structure, dislocation dynamics, and grain-boundary properties enhance the thermal stability of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed explanation applies to refractory high-entropy alloys in either as-cast or annealed states.
The relevant service regime includes temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
Mechanical loading and thermal cycling alter the governing structural mediators.
Dislocation-dominated plastic deformation governs the mechanical response.
Grain-boundary sliding governs part of the high-temperature mechanical response.
Thermal activation of dislocations governs part of the high-temperature response.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit enhanced high-temperature strength relative to conventional nickel-based superalloys.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit enhanced strength relative to conventional refractory metals.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit enhanced creep resistance relative to the stated baselines.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit enhanced thermal stability relative to the stated baselines.
The behavior depends on strain rate and alloy composition.
Irradiation, corrosion, and fatigue introduce uncertainty into the proposed behavior.
A lack of correlation between measured behavior and atomic structure, dislocation dynamics, and grain-boundary properties would falsify the hypothesis.
